title: Mounties add zapper to arsenal
article: If a Mountie pointing a M-26 Taser tells you to drop your knife and get on the ground, do it.
Do it fast and then say, "Thank you, officer."
Chances are, though, people whose minds are altered by alcohol or drugs will ignore my counsel.

Too bad for them.Because the little black Taser in the Mountie's hand packs enough punch to stop a rampaging water buffalo. All RCMP officers are being trained in their use, with several detachments now packing them.
I was among reporters treated to the absolute power of the pistol-like device yesterday during a "show-and-tell" by RCMP.
The police-issue-only Taser doesn't fire bullets, but uses "conducted energy" to incapacitate bad guys.
We got half-second bursts -- bad guys get the full five seconds.
If I wasn't held firmly in place by two officers, I would have crashed to the floor in a fetal position whimpering for my mommy.
The jolting effect of the Taser shuts all surface muscular control -- in anyone.
Even the biggest, baddest gangbanger can't tough it through a Taser burst.
Getting shot by a Taser isn't painful; it's just really, really scary. It's like an electrical current racing through your body, creating an uncontrolled spasm and then pure panic.
Imagine hooking up a car battery with jumper cables and attaching the other end to your hips. It's probably the nearest thing to getting electrocuted and staying alive.
RCMP staged this demonstration -- officers got "Tased" too -- to showcase a weapon becoming commonplace in police agencies throughout North America.

All Mounties in Manitoba will get Tasers by March. Detachments in The Pas, Thompson, Portage la Prairie and Selkirk are currently getting outfitted. RCMP in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta also have them. RCMP in New Brunswick are also being trained.
"You just got a taste of it -- five seconds is a hell of a thing," RCMP Const. John Hurly of the joint National Weapons Enforcement Support Team, said after I got zapped.
"The human body is a system of electrical impulses. This disrupts that. It causes uncontrollable muscular contractions."

More and more police are adopting the Taser as standard equipment, as it is far less likely than a gun to kill or seriously injure the victim. They cost about $800 each. Winnipeg police are currently looking at outfitting its officers with Tasers.
When hit by a Taser, an offender's muscular control ends within a second and they drop to the ground so they can be handcuffed.
There are no long-term health effects, although the memory of getting "Tased" is lasting. Trust me on that one.
The police officer, standing up to six metres away from a subject, fires the Taser much like a handgun.
Instead of a bullet, compressed nitrogen shoots two small silver probes, which are connected to the plastic weapon by high-voltage insulated wire.

When the barbed probes make contact with the target, the 26-watt taser transmits a powerful, 50,000-volt electrical pulse along the wires and into the body of the target. It can go through a five-centimetre thickness of clothing.
Hurly and RCMP trainer Sgt. Stu Beasley said police need Tasers because mace and pepper spray have limited value, especially if an offender is delusional because of a drug overdose or mental illness.
Beasley said no one can keep fighting when hit by a Taser.

Police officers could have used a Taser on Nov. 5 last year, when Winnipeg police confronted an agitated Donald Lorne Miles, 34, outside a gas station at Mountain Avenue and Salter Street. Miles was armed with a large knife and even though he was repeatedly pepper-sprayed, he refused to drop his weapon.
He was fatally shot when he lunged at one of the officers. A provincial inquest will be held into his death.
